docs.title: Volunteer Manager
docs.text: A volunteer manager for conferences, first built for BSidesCharm. Volunteers sign up on the public portal. Organizers approve them, build the schedule, send each volunteer their shifts, and check them in at the event.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
If you want to Read Run it on your own machine, test it, or change it Getting started Use the admin site to run volunteers for an event Organizer guide Deploy or operate the production site Deployment, Configuration, Secrets and keys Set up sending mail through Microsoft 365 Graph mail setup Cut a release and publish its docs Releasing Understand one part of the system Backend, Portal, Frontend, Mail relay, vol_mail Pull data from another server Export API See how the parts talk to each other Interaction diagrams See the SBOM, known vulnerabilities and bandit's findings Security Know what the lint enforces, and the security design Quality & security Look up a function the Code reference in the navigation, starting with backend.main or portal.main

The Export API guide is also written as one standalone file, site/export-api.md, on every build, to send to integrators.

docs.title: The parts
docs.text:
• Backend: the scheduler API, on PostgreSQL. The organizers' system of record.
  • Portal: the volunteer API, on SQLite. A separate application, reached by the scheduler over a signed, one-way sync API.
  • Frontend: one Vue build, serving the call for volunteers, the portal pages and the organizer app.
  • Mail relay: the only holder of the Microsoft Graph credential. It sends the portal's plain-text mail.
  • vol_mail: a command-line tool, run on an organizer's machine, that sends schedule emails with check-in QR codes.

docs.title: Building these docs
docs.text:
The published docs, one version per release, are at https://securgeek.github.io/volunteer-manager/. To build them yourself:

python3 -m pip install -r requirements-dev.txt   # includes backend/requirements.txt
mkdocs serve           # live preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000
mkdocs build --strict  # what ./run_lint.sh runs; any warning fails

Publishing a release's docs is in Releasing.

Docstrings are Google style (Args:, Returns:, Raises:). pylint's docparams check holds documented parameters to the real signature, so the reference can't silently go stale.

More detailed design notes for each service live beside the code, in the CLAUDE.md files.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
What changed in each release of Volunteer Manager. Newest first. The format follows Keep a Changelog, and versions follow Semantic Versioning. Add to Unreleased as changes land; it becomes the release's section when it's tagged (docs/operations/releasing.md).

A release that needs anything beyond the usual deploy (copy, build, restart: Deployment → Shipping a change) starts with Upgrade notes: what to do, in order, and what to check afterwards. No upgrade notes means nothing extra to do.

docs.title: Unreleased — 1.1
docs.text: Audit log, security alerts and stricter input checks.

docs.title: Upgrade notes
docs.text:
The full checklist is Deployment → Upgrading to 1.1. In short:

  1. Back up both databases, then ship the release and restart the whole stack: the backend, portal and frontend (nginx) all change and must run together. A backend without the new portal can't send alert emails.
  2. Migrations run by themselves on start: backend schema 19 → 20, portal 7 → 8. Both only add tables and columns, so the 1.0 code still runs on them if you need to roll back.
  3. .env (both optional): PORTAL_STRICT=report is the default; set AUDIT_RETENTION_DAYS for a retention other than 365 days.
  4. Alert emails start out going to the earliest organizer account only. Make sure that account has an email in Profile, tick anyone else under Security alerts in Admin → Users, then press Send test alert in Admin → Audit Log.
  5. Logs: logs/audit.log stops growing and logs/audit.jsonl takes over. Archive the old file if you like, and set up rotation for the new one (Deployment → Backups).
  6. A few days later, if Admin → Audit Log shows no portal.anomaly events from real volunteers, set PORTAL_STRICT=enforce and restart the portal.

If you ran a pre-release 1.1 build: its users.audit_access is replaced by users.audit_alerts, ticked on the earliest organizer only. Re-tick anyone else.

Developers: tools/gather-screenshots now needs Node 22.12 or later.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Audit log (Admin → Audit Log, for every organizer). Every sign-in and failed attempt, account and role change, schedule and volunteer change, export API call and refused request is recorded and searchable: filter by kind of event, severity, who, address, site or text, and expand a row for its details. Written to logs/audit.jsonl and to the new audit_events table.
  • Security alert emails to the organizers ticked under Security alerts in Admin → Users: bursts of failed sign-ins and password sprays; new or changed accounts and roles; someone else's password, passkeys or reset address changed; a new email key or export API key; sign-ins or key use from a new network; attack patterns in requests; and input the volunteer pages could never send. At most once an hour per cause, then a summary of anything held back. Send test alert checks the mail path end to end.
  • Request watching in the backend and the portal (security_signals.py, the same file in both): SQL and script injection, path traversal, scanners and probing, cross-site writes and forged session cookies. It only watches; the portal's findings reach the backend's audit log over the sync API.
  • Strict input rules shared by the volunteer pages (frontend/src/lib/portal_rules.js) and the portal (portal/validation.py), held together by one list of test cases. Input that breaks them is a portal.anomaly: alerted on, and refused when PORTAL_STRICT=enforce.
  • Settings AUDIT_RETENTION_DAYS (default 365) and PORTAL_STRICT (default report).
  • Docs: Deployment → Upgrading to 1.1, audit-log rotation, an architecture diagram from a hostile request to an alert, and the organizer guide to the audit log and alerts.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• The audit log is structured JSON (logs/audit.jsonl); the free-text logs/audit.log is no longer written.
  • The sign-in page says how long to wait after too many wrong passwords, instead of "Invalid username or password".
  • The volunteer pages explain a bad name, handle, email or answer in the form before sending, and say so when a sign-in link is damaged.
  • The docs site is titled Volunteer Manager; the conference is spelled "BSidesCharm" throughout, and the maintenance page no longer names a conference.
  • tools/gather-screenshots moves to puppeteer-core 25 and needs Node 22.12+; it reinstalls its packages when its lock file changes.
  • Schema: backend 20 (audit_events, users.audit_alerts), portal 8 (portal_security_events). Both migrate on start.
  • nginx caps volunteer-portal request bodies at 64 KB.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• A username containing a NUL character crashed sign-in with a server error; any request carrying one is now refused with a 400.
  • sessions.ip_addr recorded the proxy's address instead of the client's.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• The old audit log wrote a failed sign-in's username verbatim, so one containing a newline could forge log lines. Every line is now JSON with non-ASCII escaped.
  • Failed password sign-ins are rate limited, per username and address (successes never count, so a check-in desk on the venue network can't lock itself out).
  • Sign-in no longer reveals which usernames exist through response time.
  • Alert emails are defanged (details an attacker typed can't arrive as clickable links) and have their own hourly mail allowance, apart from password resets.
  • tools/gather-screenshots: six Dependabot alerts closed (extract-zip, basic-ftp, zod).

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• The portal's code reference named the database setting PORTAL_DB_PATH; it's PORTAL_DB.
  • CSV imports say why a row wasn't saved in plain words, rather than the database's message.
  • A failed invite email says it couldn't be sent and to copy the link.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: • CodeQL fixes: the portal's verify page shows only a real token's shape, HTML-escaped; the email and link patterns can't backtrack on hostile input; the plain-text email renderer caps alt text and addresses.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• README screenshots, and tools/gather-screenshots to retake them on a throwaway demo stack.
  • Refreshed interaction diagrams, including the export API.

docs.title: 1.0.0 — 2026-11-21
docs.text: First release: the volunteer portal (call for volunteers, email-first signup with magic-link sign-in, shift picking, self-service changes), the organizer app (schedule builder and editor, approvals, assignment, schedule emails with check-in QR codes, check-in, radios, notes and ratings, passkey or password sign-in with roles), the read-only export API, and email addresses stored only encrypted to an offline key.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: This page takes you from a fresh clone to the whole stack running on your machine. It then covers the tests, the lint and these docs. Deploying to the real server is in Deployment.

docs.title: What's in the repo
docs.text:
Directory What it is Runs as backend/ The scheduler API (FastAPI, PostgreSQL). Organizers' data and every write. backend container portal/ The volunteer portal API (FastAPI, SQLite). Signup and volunteer sign-in. portal container frontend/ The Vue 3 site. One build serves the call for volunteers, the portal pages and the organizer app. frontend container (nginx) mailrelay/ Sends the portal's mail through Microsoft Graph. Standard library only. mailrelay container tools/vol_mail/ Sends schedule emails from an organizer's own machine. not a container maintenance/ The "back soon" page shown while the stack is down. its own compose project docs/ This site. not deployed

Services has one page per service, and the interaction diagrams show how they talk to each other.

docs.title: Run the stack
docs.text:
You need podman with podman-compose, or Docker with Compose.

  1. Copy the settings file and fill in the secrets:

    cp .env.example .env
openssl rand -hex 32      # once each for EMAIL_HMAC_KEY and SYNC_SECRET

    The portal refuses to start without EMAIL_HMAC_KEY, SYNC_KEY_ID and SYNC_SECRET. Leave MAIL_BACKEND=file for now: sign-in links are then written as .eml files to logs/portal_mail/ instead of being sent. Every setting is described in Configuration.

  2. Build and start everything:

    podman-compose up -d --build        # or: docker compose up -d --build

  3. Open http://localhost:8080. The admin site sends you to the setup wizard, which creates the first organizer account and then sets up the schedule and the volunteer roster. The organizer guide walks through it.

Port 8080 (FRONTEND_PORT) serves the whole site. Port 8082 (PORTAL_SITE_PORT) serves only the public pages, as the public hostname does once deployed. Both listen on 127.0.0.1 only.

The mail relay exits at startup until its Graph settings are filled in. That's expected with MAIL_BACKEND=file, and nothing else depends on it.

docs.title: Volunteer email addresses
docs.text:
Addresses are encrypted in the browser to an RSA key pair that only organizers hold. Signup stays closed until the public key is uploaded. To try signup locally, make a throwaway pair and upload public.pem under Admin → Email Key:

openssl genpkey -algorithm RSA -pkeyopt rsa_keygen_bits:3072 -out private.pem
openssl pkey -in private.pem -pubout -out public.pem

Both files are ignored by git and kept off the server. Secrets explains why.

docs.title: The frontend dev server
docs.text:
To work on the frontend with hot reload, keep the containers running and start Vite:

cd frontend && npm install && npm run dev

Vite sends /api/portal/* to the portal and the rest of /api/* to the backend (vite.config.js).

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
The backend and the portal are separate applications, and both have modules named db and main, so each suite runs in its own pytest process:

Work in a virtual environment. requirements-dev.txt pulls in the backend's requirements too, since some tests and the docs build import the backend:

python3 -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
./run_tests.sh                     # portal, backend and vol_mail, one process each
(cd mailrelay && python3 -m pytest)

Most backend tests need a real PostgreSQL, and they drop the target database's schema. Point them at a throwaway one:

podman run -d --rm --name bsides-testpg -p 127.0.0.1:55432:5432 \
  -e POSTGRES_DB=scheduler_test -e POSTGRES_USER=scheduler -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=test \
  docker.io/library/postgres:18-alpine

TEST_PG_HOST=127.0.0.1 TEST_PG_PORT=55432 TEST_PG_DB=scheduler_test \
TEST_PG_USER=scheduler TEST_PG_PASSWORD=test ./run_tests.sh

Without TEST_PG_HOST, those tests are skipped. The tests need no network, no mail server and no browser. Graph, the portal's side of sync and passkey authenticators are faked.

docs.title: Lint and docs
docs.text:
./run_lint.sh              # pylint per app, bandit, and mkdocs build --strict (in the venv)
./run_lint.sh --no-docs    # also --no-pylint, --no-bandit; --todo lists TODO/FIXME
mkdocs serve               # this site at http://127.0.0.1:8000

The lint is strict about a few things, and the rest is a score that may only go up. Quality & security explains the rules. Two of them come up in almost every change:

  • SQL is always a complete literal with bound parameters. Nothing builds SQL text, not even from constants.
  • Docstrings are Google style (Args:, Returns:, Raises:). The code reference is built from them, and pylint checks that a documented parameter list matches the signature.

docs.title: Volunteer Manager Export API
docs.text:
A read-only HTTPS API for other servers. It returns the volunteer schedule and the volunteer list with each person's shifts. Every endpoint is GET, and none of them can change anything.

Base URL: https://<admin hostname>, which the organizers give you with your key

Call it from a server. It sends no CORS headers, so a web page on another site can't call it from the browser.

docs.title: 1. Getting a key
docs.text:
An organizer creates a key for you and sends it over once. It can't be shown again, so store it like a password. Send it on every request:

Authorization: Bearer bsc_…
  • Keys expire. The default is 30 days and the longest is 365. Ask for a new key before yours runs out. There is no renewal: you get a new key and the old one is revoked.
  • A key may be locked to IP addresses or CIDR ranges. If your server's outbound address changes, ask for a new key with the updated list.
  • One key per app or person, so one can be revoked without affecting the others.
  • Scopes decide what a key can read:
Scope Grants schedule:read GET /api/export/schedule volunteers:read GET /api/export/volunteers volunteers:email Adds email_enc to each volunteer. This is RSA-OAEP/SHA-256 ciphertext in base64, and it can't be read without the organizers' private key. checkin:codes Adds checkin_code to each shift.

Most integrations need schedule:read and volunteers:read, and nothing else.

docs.title: 2. Errors
docs.text: Status Meaning 401 {"detail": "Unauthorized"} The key is missing, unknown, expired or revoked, it lacks the scope, or your IP isn't allowed. The response is the same in every case, on purpose. 429 Ten failed attempts from your address within 15 minutes. Wait, then fix the key. Retrying won't help. 400 A query parameter with a value it doesn't accept, such as status=bogus. 422 A query parameter of the wrong type, such as assigned=maybe. The body says which.

docs.title: 3. Conventions
docs.text:
Every response starts with generated_at (server time, UTC), event_title and event_tz. The tables in sections 4 and 5 list every field; these are the rules that apply across them.

Names - name is First L., or Handle [First L.] when the volunteer gave a handle. - The parts are also given separately as first_name, last_initial and handle. Any of them may be "".

Times - time is the shift label as the organizers wrote it, for example "0800-1200". - start and end are ISO-8601 in the event timezone, with its offset, for example "2027-04-24T08:00:00-04:00". - start and end are null when the day has no date set, or when the label isn't a time range. - date is YYYY-MM-DD, or null.

Identifiers - slot_key (day_time_position, for example sat_0800_sec3) identifies one slot. It stays the same as long as the schedule's structure doesn't change. - vol_id is a string. Treat it as opaque.

Booleans in query strings accept 1/0 and true/false.

Scoped fields (email_enc, checkin_code) are left out entirely when the key lacks the scope. With the scope, they are always present, and may be null.

docs.title: 4. GET /api/export/schedule
docs.text:
Returns every slot in time order, filled or not.

Needs the schedule:read scope.

Parameter Type Default Effect assigned boolean false Only slots with a volunteer. day string or null — Only one day, by day_key, for example sat. An unknown day_key returns an empty list, not an error.

Response

Field Type Description generated_at string Server time of the response, ISO-8601 UTC. event_title string The event's title from App Settings. event_tz string IANA timezone that start and end are given in. slots array of Slot Every slot in time order.

Each item in slots (Slot)

Field Type Description slot_key string day_time_position. Stable while the schedule's structure is unchanged. day_key string The day's key. day string The day's label. date string or null YYYY-MM-DD, or null when the day has no date. time_key string The time's key. time string The shift label as the organizers wrote it. start string or null ISO-8601 in the event timezone, with its offset. Null when the day has no date or time isn't a range. end string or null Like start. A range past midnight ends the next day. pos_key string The position's key. position string The position's label. category string The position's category. vol_id string The assigned volunteer, or "" when the slot is empty. Opaque. checked_in boolean Whether the volunteer has checked in. Always false for an empty slot. name string The volunteer's display name, or "" when the slot is empty.

Example response

{
  "generated_at": "2027-04-20T14:03:11.402Z",
  "event_title": "BSidesCharm 2027",
  "event_tz": "America/New_York",
  "slots": [
    {
      "slot_key": "sat_0800_sec3",
      "day_key": "sat",
      "day": "Saturday",
      "date": "2027-04-24",
      "time_key": "0800",
      "time": "0800-1200",
      "start": "2027-04-24T08:00:00-04:00",
      "end": "2027-04-24T12:00:00-04:00",
      "pos_key": "sec3",
      "position": "Security 3",
      "category": "Security",
      "vol_id": "1042",
      "checked_in": false,
      "name": "Zero Cool [Jim E.]"
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: 5. GET /api/export/volunteers
docs.text:
Returns every volunteer, sorted by name, with their shifts in time order.

Needs the volunteers:read scope.

Parameter Type Default Effect status string "active" active: approved, and neither cancelled nor inactive. all: everyone, including pending signups; check status, cancelled and inactive. Anything else is a 400. assigned boolean false Only volunteers with at least one shift.

Response

Field Type Description generated_at string Server time of the response, ISO-8601 UTC. event_title string The event's title from App Settings. event_tz string IANA timezone that start and end are given in. volunteers array of Volunteer Volunteers sorted by name.

Each item in volunteers (Volunteer)

Field Type Description vol_id string The volunteer's id. Opaque. name string First L., or Handle [First L.] with a handle. first_name string May be "". last_initial string May be "". handle string May be "". status string pending (signed up, not yet approved) or active. cancelled boolean The volunteer cancelled. inactive boolean An organizer set the volunteer inactive. shifts array of Shift Shifts in time order; [] when none. email_enc string or null Only with the volunteers:email scope. The email address, RSA-OAEP/SHA-256 encrypted to the organizers' key, base64. Null when none is on file.

Each item in shifts (Shift)

Field Type Description slot_key string day_time_position. Stable while the schedule's structure is unchanged. day_key string The day's key. day string The day's label. date string or null YYYY-MM-DD, or null when the day has no date. time_key string The time's key. time string The shift label as the organizers wrote it. start string or null ISO-8601 in the event timezone, with its offset. Null when the day has no date or time isn't a range. end string or null Like start. A range past midnight ends the next day. pos_key string The position's key. position string The position's label. category string The position's category. checked_in boolean Whether the volunteer has checked in. checkin_code string or null Only with the checkin:codes scope. The check-in code mailed to the volunteer as a QR code.

Example response

{
  "generated_at": "2027-04-20T14:03:11.402Z",
  "event_title": "BSidesCharm 2027",
  "event_tz": "America/New_York",
  "volunteers": [
    {
      "vol_id": "1042",
      "name": "Zero Cool [Jim E.]",
      "first_name": "Jim",
      "last_initial": "E",
      "handle": "Zero Cool",
      "status": "active",
      "cancelled": false,
      "inactive": false,
      "shifts": [
        {
          "slot_key": "sat_0800_sec3",
          "day_key": "sat",
          "day": "Saturday",
          "date": "2027-04-24",
          "time_key": "0800",
          "time": "0800-1200",
          "start": "2027-04-24T08:00:00-04:00",
          "end": "2027-04-24T12:00:00-04:00",
          "pos_key": "sec3",
          "position": "Security 3",
          "category": "Security",
          "checked_in": false
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

The example leaves out the scoped fields. A key with volunteers:email also gets email_enc on each volunteer, and one with checkin:codes gets checkin_code on each shift.

docs.title: 6. Examples
docs.text:
curl

export VOLUNTEER_API_KEY='bsc_…'
BASE=https://<admin hostname>

curl -sf -H "Authorization: Bearer $VOLUNTEER_API_KEY" \
  "$BASE/api/export/schedule?assigned=1" | jq '.slots[] | {start, position, name}'

curl -sf -H "Authorization: Bearer $VOLUNTEER_API_KEY" \
  "$BASE/api/export/volunteers?assigned=1" | jq '.volunteers[] | {name, shifts: (.shifts | length)}'

Python (standard library only)

import json, os, urllib.request

BASE = "https://<admin hostname>"

def export(path, **params):
    query = "&".join(f"{k}={v}" for k, v in params.items())
    req = urllib.request.Request(
        f"{BASE}{path}?{query}",
        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['VOLUNTEER_API_KEY']}"},
    )
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=15) as r:
        return json.load(r)

for slot in export("/api/export/schedule", assigned=1)["slots"]:
    print(slot["start"], slot["position"], slot["name"])

docs.title: 7. Fair use
docs.text:
• There's no rate limit on successful calls. Polling every few minutes is fine. Polling every second isn't.
  • Use generated_at to see how fresh a response is.
  • Every call is logged under the key's label. Failed calls are logged too.
  • If a key leaks, tell the organizers so they can revoke it right away.

docs.title: Object interaction diagrams
docs.text:
How the BSides services, and the main objects inside them, talk to each other. Each diagram is drawn from the code and compose.yml. The names are real: routes, functions, tables and columns.

# Diagram Read it when you're changing… 1 Deployment and trust boundaries compose, nginx, the tunnel, anything network-facing 2 An organizer change any backend write endpoint 3 One portal sync tick portal_sync.py, portal/routers/sync.py 4 Volunteer signup portal/routers/signup.py, auth.py, the /apply pages 5 Approval and the push back routers/portal_admin.py, the volunteer push 6 An export API call api_auth.py, routers/export.py 7 A schedule email round email_template.py, tools/vol_mail/ 8 Shift check-in checkin_codes.py, routers/checkin.py 9 Admin invite and reset mail invites.py, password_reset.py, send_admin_mail 10 Who owns which volunteer column any volunteer column, either side 11 An early-access invite routers/portal_admin.py invites, signup_invites on either side 12 Purging a volunteer purge_volunteers on either side, any table holding a vol_id 13 Passkey sign-in routers/passkeys.py, auth.start_session, lib/passkey.js 14 From a hostile request to an alert security_signals.py, portal/validation.py, audit.py, alerts.py

The diagrams are Mermaid. They render on this site, on GitHub, and in VS Code's Markdown preview with a Mermaid extension. If a diagram and the code disagree, the code is right: fix the diagram in the same change.

docs.title: 1. Deployment and trust boundaries
docs.text:
Everything runs under podman-compose on one host. The only way in from the internet is a tunnel: its client runs on the host, outside compose, and dials the frontend's two loopback-only ports. Thick lines are internet-facing.

flowchart LR
    subgraph internet["Internet"]
        vol["Volunteer browser"]
        org["Organizer browser"]
        integ["Integrator server"]
        graph_api["Microsoft Graph"]
        cf["Edge<br/>TLS, access gate"]
    end

    subgraph orgbox["An organizer's machine"]
        volmail["tools/vol_mail<br/>+ private.pem"]
    end

    subgraph host["Host"]
        cfd["tunnel client<br/>(not in compose)"]

        subgraph default_net["podman-compose network: default"]
            nginx["frontend: nginx<br/>:8080 full site<br/>:8082 portal only<br/>host 127.0.0.1 only"]
            backend["backend: FastAPI :5000<br/>scheduler"]
            pg[("postgres 18<br/>pgdata18")]
            portal["portal: FastAPI :5001<br/>no host port"]
            pdb[("SQLite<br/>portal.db")]
        end

        subgraph mail_internal["network: mail_internal (internal)"]
            relay["mailrelay :5002<br/>Graph refresh token"]
        end
    end

    vol ==>|"public host<br/>/apply, /api/portal"| cf
    org ==>|"admin host<br/>after the gate's sign-in"| cf
    integ ==>|"admin host /api/export/*<br/>gate bypass, bearer key"| cf
    volmail ==>|"export API<br/>volunteers:email, checkin:codes"| cf

    cf ==>|"tunnel"| cfd
    cfd -->|"public host → :8082"| nginx
    cfd -->|"admin host → :8080"| nginx
    nginx -->|"/api/portal/*<br/>(both servers)"| portal
    nginx -->|"/api/*<br/>(:8080 only)"| backend
    backend --> pg
    portal --> pdb

    backend -->|"signed sync API<br/>http://portal:5001<br/>scheduler is always the client"| portal
    portal -->|"POST /send, bearer token"| relay
    relay ==>|"mail_egress: /me/sendMail"| graph_api

    volmail ==>|"device-code sign-in, sendMail"| graph_api

Points the picture makes:

  • The portal never calls the scheduler. All sync traffic is scheduler → portal, so the scheduler needs no inbound route.
  • The public hostname can't reach the scheduler. nginx's :8082 server serves the SPA and /api/portal/* only; /admin and every other /api/* are a 404 there, and /api/sync/* isn't under /api/portal/. The organizer side is on its own hostname behind an access gate, with /api/export/* let through for servers, which carry their own bearer keys.
  • Only the mail relay holds the Graph credential. It sits on an internal-only network that the portal shares. Its own egress network reaches Microsoft and nothing else.
  • private.pem never reaches the host. Email addresses are only decrypted on an organizer's machine, by vol_mail or by the browser (Volunteers tab → Decrypt).
  • Client IPs: nginx takes the client IP from the edge's client-IP header, which the edge sets, and passes it on as a single X-Forwarded-For value (portal/CLAUDE.md → Auth invariants).
  • Nothing but the frontend publishes a host port, and only on 127.0.0.1, so plain HTTP isn't reachable from the LAN.

docs.title: 2. An organizer change
docs.text:
Any write in the organizer app, for example assigning a volunteer to a slot. The same tail end runs for every schedule mutation: browsers learn about it over SSE, and the portal gets it on the next push.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor O as Organizer
    participant FE as Admin SPA
    participant NG as nginx
    participant R as routers/schedule.py
    participant DB as db.py
    participant PG as Postgres
    participant EV as routers/events.py
    participant PS as portal_sync

    O->>FE: assign volunteer to slot
    FE->>NG: POST /api/assign_vol (FormData, session cookie)
    NG->>R: proxy
    R->>DB: Depends(get_db) borrows a pooled connection
    R->>DB: Depends(RoleChecker("organizer"))
    DB->>DB: get_session_data: _session_cache, else sessions table
    alt not signed in, or wrong role
        DB-->>FE: 401 or 403
    end
    R->>PG: UPDATE schedule SET vol_id = ? WHERE ...
    R->>PG: COMMIT
    R->>EV: broadcast("assignment")
    EV->>PS: request_push()
    PS-->>PS: sets _state.push_event (thread-safe)
    EV-->>FE: SSE "assignment" to every open /api/events stream
    R->>DB: audit(request, ...)
    R->>PG: _build_schedule (full schedule)
    R-->>FE: 200 with the updated schedule
    Note over PS: The sync loop wakes, waits PUSH_DEBOUNCE (2 s) so a burst<br/>of edits pushes once, then runs a tick (diagram 3).

docs.title: 3. One portal sync tick
docs.text:
portal_sync._sync_once, every PORTAL_SYNC_INTERVAL seconds (30), or sooner when request_push() wakes it. Every request is signed. The portal rejects any failure with the same bare 401.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant L as portal_sync loop
    participant PG as Postgres
    participant SEC as portal security.py
    participant P as portal routers/sync.py
    participant SQ as portal.db

    Note over L,P: Each request carries x-sync-key-id, -timestamp, -nonce, -signature<br/>signing METHOD, path, timestamp, nonce, sha256(body)
    L->>P: GET /api/sync/heartbeat
    P->>SEC: verify signature, ±300 s window, nonce unseen
    P->>SQ: INSERT sync_nonces (replay guard)
    P-->>L: revs, snapshot_hash, branding_hash, hmac_key_fp, pubkey_fp

    opt volunteers_rev > our cursor
        L->>P: GET /api/sync/volunteers?since=cursor (pages of 500)
        P-->>L: changed volunteers and their picks
        L->>PG: skip a row that is the old id of a pending re-key
        L->>PG: dirty row: volunteer-owned columns only, else upsert the whole row
        L->>PG: mark the signup_invites row used when invite_id comes back
        L->>PG: raise shift_flags for dropped assigned picks, replace vol_picks
        L-->>L: broadcast("volunteers") when anything was written
    end

    opt rows with portal_dirty
        L->>P: POST /api/sync/volunteers (rekeys first, then upserts, op_id)
        P->>SQ: static upsert, only the columns sent
        P-->>L: written, renamed
        L->>PG: clear portal_dirty where status still matches what was sent
    end

    L->>P: GET /api/sync/config
    P-->>L: the portal's settings
    opt settings differ
        L->>P: POST /api/sync/settings (portal_signup_open, email_pubkey if fp differs)
    end

    L->>PG: build_snapshot (days, times, day_times with remaining, positions, slots)
    opt snapshot content_hash differs
        L->>P: POST /api/sync/schedule (op_id)
        P->>SQ: BEGIN IMMEDIATE, replace each snapshot table, COMMIT
    end

    opt branding hash differs
        L->>P: POST /api/sync/branding (title, logos, favicon, contact links)
    end

    L->>PG: build_content (landing, questionnaire, invite email)
    opt heartbeat has content_hash and it differs
        L->>P: POST /api/sync/content (op_id)
    end

    L->>PG: build_invites (early-access invite hashes, diagram 11)
    opt heartbeat has invites_hash and it differs
        L->>P: POST /api/sync/signup_invites (op_id), replaces the portal's list
    end

    L->>PG: portal_sync_state: mark ok, or record the error
    Note over L: Any exception ends the tick as failed. The loop logs on the<br/>transition only and tries again next tick.

Every POST carries an op_id. The portal stores the result in sync_ops and replays it for a repeat, so a push that timed out after the portal committed can be retried safely.

docs.title: 4. Volunteer signup
docs.text:
Email first. The portal can only ever mail an address someone has just shown they know, because nothing in it can decrypt email_enc.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor V as Volunteer
    participant SPA as /apply pages
    participant S as portal signup.py and auth.py
    participant SQ as portal.db
    participant M as mailer.py
    participant MR as mailrelay
    participant G as Microsoft Graph

    V->>SPA: enter email (and the ?invite= token, if the link carried one)
    SPA->>S: POST /api/portal/signup/check_email {email, invite}
    S->>S: email_hmac = HMAC(EMAIL_HMAC_KEY, normalize(email))
    S->>SQ: ratelimit.check per IP and per address
    alt over the limit
        S-->>SPA: 429
    else already registered
        S-->>SPA: "sign in instead" (goes to request_link)
    else signup closed and no live invite, or full
        S-->>SPA: 409 closed or full
    else no email_pubkey
        S-->>SPA: 409 closed
    else open, or a live invite
        S->>S: email_enc = RSA-OAEP(email_pubkey, email)
        S->>SQ: INSERT login_tokens (sha256 of token, purpose signup, invite_id)
        S->>M: send magic link {PORTAL_PUBLIC_URL}/apply/verify?t=...
        M->>MR: POST /send {to, subject, body}, bearer MAIL_RELAY_TOKEN
        MR->>G: /me/sendMail, from MAIL_SENDER (set at startup)
        S-->>SPA: check your mail
    end
    Note over S: Every reply waits out the same floor, so timing doesn't<br/>tell one outcome from another. The invite isn't spent here.

    V->>SPA: open the link at /apply/verify
    Note over SPA: Loading the page spends nothing:<br/>mail scanners and link previews fetch links.
    V->>SPA: confirm
    SPA->>S: POST /api/portal/verify {t}
    S->>SQ: conditional UPDATE consumes the token (rowcount decides a race)
    S->>SQ: INSERT session (hash only), vol_id NULL means signup session
    S-->>SPA: session cookie

    SPA->>S: GET signup/fields, GET timeslots (remaining, overlaps)
    SPA->>S: POST signup/check_name
    S-->>SPA: possible_match only
    V->>SPA: answers, two prefs, extras
    SPA->>S: POST /api/portal/signup/submit
    S->>SQ: BEGIN IMMEDIATE
    S->>SQ: address already has a volunteer row?
    S->>SQ: _consume_invite: conditional UPDATE signup_invites SET used_at
    S->>SQ: re-check open (or the invite), re-check picks
    S->>SQ: INSERT volunteers p-xxxxxxxx status pending, invite_id, vol_picks
    alt already signed up, or the unique index on email_hmac (two submits raced)
        S-->>SPA: 409 already signed up
    else closed and the invite is gone
        S-->>SPA: 409
    else a pick filled meanwhile
        S-->>SPA: 409, detail.full names it, the form reopens the shifts step
    else ok
        S->>SQ: remaining minus 1 for the two prefs
        S->>SQ: upgrade the session in place to this vol_id, COMMIT
        S-->>SPA: signed up, pending
    end
    Note over S,SQ: Any 409 rolls the whole transaction back, the invite's use with it.
    Note over S,SQ: Next sync tick (diagram 3): volunteers_rev moved, so the scheduler<br/>pulls the pending row and its picks into Postgres.

docs.title: 5. Approval and the push back
docs.text:
An organizer approves a pending signup, optionally giving it a badge number. The request doesn't call the portal itself: portal_dirty marks the row, and request_push() wakes the sync loop, which carries it about PUSH_DEBOUNCE (2 s) later. If the portal is down, the row stays dirty and every later tick retries it.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor O as Organizer
    participant A as routers/portal_admin.py
    participant PG as Postgres
    participant L as portal_sync loop
    participant P as portal routers/sync.py
    participant SQ as portal.db

    O->>A: POST /api/admin/portal/approve {vol_id, new_vol_id?}
    A->>PG: _pending: status pending, not cancelled or inactive
    alt badge number given
        A->>PG: refuse if the vol_id has schedule, vol_notes or radio rows (one EXISTS query)
        A->>PG: copy the row under new_vol_id, status active, portal_rekey_from = old id
        A->>PG: move vol_picks, delete the old row
    else no badge number
        A->>PG: UPDATE status active, portal_dirty TRUE
    end
    A->>PG: COMMIT, audit
    A->>L: portal_sync.request_push()
    A-->>O: ok, final vol_id
    Note over PG: is_assignable is now TRUE (a generated column),<br/>so the volunteer appears in every picker.

    L->>P: tick after the debounce: POST /api/sync/volunteers
    Note right of L: rekeys first (old to new vol_id), then the dirty rows<br/>with scheduler-owned columns only
    P->>SQ: rename vol_id in sessions, login_tokens, vol_picks, snapshot_slots
    P->>SQ: upsert: CASE WHEN sent per column, so unsent columns keep their value
    P-->>L: written, renamed
    L->>PG: clear portal_dirty only where status still equals what was sent
    Note over L,PG: While a row is dirty, a pull takes only the volunteer-owned columns, and<br/>skips the old id of a pending re-key outright, so the portal's older copy<br/>can't undo a decision that hasn't reached the portal yet.

docs.title: 6. An export API call
docs.text:
A server, or vol_mail, reads the schedule or the volunteers with a bearer key. Every refusal looks the same.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Caller (server or vol_mail)
    participant NG as nginx
    participant T as api_auth.TokenChecker(scope)
    participant E as routers/export.py
    participant PG as Postgres

    C->>NG: GET /api/export/volunteers?status=active<br/>Authorization: Bearer bsc_...
    NG->>T: proxy (client IP = first X-Forwarded-For hop, and nginx sends just one)
    T->>T: _over_limit(ip)? 10 failures in 15 min, keyed by rate_key (IPv6 by its /64)
    alt over the limit
        T-->>C: 429
    end
    T->>PG: SELECT ... FROM api_tokens WHERE token_hash = sha256(key)<br/>AND not revoked AND not expired
    alt no row, scope missing, or IP not in allowed_ips
        T->>T: _record_fail(ip)
        T->>T: audit "Export API refused"
        T-->>C: 401 {"detail": "Unauthorized"} (the same in every case)
    end
    T->>PG: UPDATE last_used_at, last_used_ip, COMMIT
    T->>T: audit under the key's label and id, never the key
    T->>E: key row with scopes
    E->>PG: _slots: one query for every slot, with check-in state
    E->>PG: volunteers WHERE (? OR v.is_assignable)
    opt key has checkin:codes
        E->>E: checkin_codes.make_code per shift
    end
    E->>E: response_model VolunteersExport, exclude_unset<br/>(email_enc only with volunteers:email)
    E-->>C: 200 JSON

The caller's guide, with every field, is the Export API page, generated from the same response models.

docs.title: 7. A schedule email round
docs.text:
The site never sends schedule email. It provides the template and the data; vol_mail, on an organizer's machine, decrypts the addresses and sends. Usually a draft round, then a final.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor O as Organizer
    participant SITE as Scheduler (email_template.py)
    participant VM as vol_mail.py
    participant EX as Export API
    participant KEY as private.pem
    participant G as Microsoft Graph

    O->>SITE: write the template (Markdown, images), preview as any volunteer
    O->>SITE: GET /api/email_template/package
    SITE-->>O: zip: HTML and text with placeholders, assets, manifest with sha256

    O->>VM: vol_mail.py fetch
    VM->>EX: GET /api/export/volunteers?assigned=1 (diagram 6)
    EX-->>VM: volunteers with email_enc and checkin_code per shift
    VM->>VM: box.json, mode 0600

    O->>VM: vol_mail.py preview (one volunteer)
    VM-->>O: .eml, .html, .txt with real codes and QR images

    O->>VM: vol_mail.py send --round draft --dry-run
    VM->>KEY: decrypt each email_enc (RSA-OAEP)
    VM->>VM: skip any that don't decrypt or aren't a plain address, and report them
    VM->>VM: write the plan: recipients + sha256 of package and box

    O->>VM: vol_mail.py send --round draft
    VM->>VM: refuse if the package or box changed since the dry run
    VM->>VM: skip anyone already in this round's sent log
    VM-->>O: "Type send to continue"
    VM->>G: device-code sign-in (kept in memory only)
    loop each recipient
        VM->>KEY: decrypt email_enc
        VM->>G: sendMail (HTML, inline QR images) as MAIL_SENDER
        VM->>VM: append to the round's sent log
    end

docs.title: 8. Shift check-in
docs.text:
The QR code in the email is an HMAC over the slot and the volunteer. A valid code isn't enough on its own: the volunteer must still be assigned to that slot.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor D as Check-in desk
    participant SC as BarcodeScanner.vue
    participant CK as routers/checkin.py
    participant CC as checkin_codes.py
    participant PG as Postgres

    D->>SC: scan QR (or type the code)
    SC->>CK: POST /api/checkin/scan {code, force}
    CK->>CK: RoleChecker organizer or checkin
    CK->>PG: app_kv.checkin_key
    CK->>CC: verify_code(key, "BSC1.slot_key.b64(vol_id).mac")
    alt bad MAC or malformed
        CC-->>D: 400
    end
    CK->>CK: record_checkin(vol_id, slot_key, force), the one check-in path
    CK->>PG: is vol_id still assigned to slot_key?
    alt reassigned since the email went out
        CK-->>D: 409
    end
    CK->>CC: shift_start(event_date, time_str, event_tz)
    CK->>PG: already a [CheckIn] note?
    alt already checked in
        CK-->>D: already: true, nothing written
    end
    alt over 45 min early or 10 min late, and not force
        CK-->>D: needs_confirm, nothing written
        D->>SC: Check in anyway
        SC->>CK: POST /api/checkin/scan {code, force: true}
    end
    CK->>PG: INSERT vol_notes "[CheckIn] | slot_key"
    opt forced early or late
        CK->>PG: INSERT vol_notes "[CheckInTiming] Early or Late N min | slot_key"
    end
    CK-->>D: checked in

Rotating the key (POST /api/checkin/rotate_key) changes checkin_key, which voids every code already mailed.

docs.title: 9. Admin invite and reset mail
docs.text:
The scheduler has no mail path of its own. It asks the portal, through the one narrow endpoint that mails an address the portal didn't verify itself. That endpoint takes four kinds: invite and reset (drawn here), signup_invite (diagram 11) and alert (diagram 14).

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor O as Organizer
    participant B as backend invites.py or password_reset.py
    participant PG as Postgres
    participant PS as portal_sync.send_admin_mail
    participant P as portal routers/sync.py
    participant M as Mailer.send_admin
    participant MR as mailrelay
    participant G as Microsoft Graph

    O->>B: POST /api/invites {role, email} (or someone: POST password_reset/request)
    B->>PG: INSERT user_invites: sha256(token), expires NOW() + ? * INTERVAL
    B->>PS: kind invite, address, link {site_origin()}/admin/invite?t=...
    Note right of B: site_origin() is ADMIN_PUBLIC_URL,<br/>else PORTAL_PUBLIC_URL (one origin)
    PS->>P: POST /api/sync/send_admin_mail (signed, op_id)
    P->>P: link must start with its own ADMIN_PUBLIC_URL + /admin/invite?t= or /admin/reset?t=
    P->>P: one address, strict pattern, at most 20 admin mails an hour
    P->>M: fixed template admin_invite.txt or admin_reset.txt
    M->>MR: POST /send
    MR->>G: /me/sendMail
    P->>P: audit "admin_mail.sent", detail invite (no address, no link)
    P-->>PS: ok
    alt mail failed
        B-->>O: invite created, email_error, copy the link yourself
    else sent
        B-->>O: invite created, emailed
    end
    Note over B,O: Password reset always returns the same reply (GENERIC),<br/>whatever happened. Failures go to the log and the audit trail.

docs.title: 10. Who owns which volunteer column
docs.text:
A volunteer exists in both databases. Each column has exactly one owner, and each side only ever sends the columns it owns. That's what lets an approval waiting to go out and an edit the volunteer just made both survive.

flowchart LR
    subgraph portal_side["Portal owns (volunteer's own edits)"]
        vo["time_pref, add_time, add_any<br/>answers, vol_picks<br/>cancelled_at"]
    end
    subgraph sched_side["Scheduler owns (organizer decisions)"]
        so["status (pending, active)<br/>name<br/>inactive_at"]
    end
    subgraph derived["Derived in Postgres (generated columns)"]
        gc["is_live = not cancelled and not inactive<br/>is_counted = pending or active, and live<br/>is_assignable = active and live"]
    end

    vo -->|"pull: always taken,<br/>even on a dirty row"| pgv[("Postgres volunteers")]
    so -->|"push: only these columns,<br/>CASE WHEN sent per column"| pv[("portal.db volunteers")]
    pgv --> gc
    gc -->|"pickers, capacity,<br/>needs-replacement flags"| uses["schedule.py, volunteers.py,<br/>portal_admin.py, export.py,<br/>portal_sync.compute_remaining"]

Defined in portal_sync.VOLUNTEER_OWNED / SCHEDULER_OWNED (scheduler side) and routers/sync.PUSH_COLUMNS (portal side). cancelled_at isn't in the portal's push columns at all, so the scheduler can neither set nor clear it.

docs.title: 11. An early-access invite
docs.text:
A single-use link that lets one person sign up while the call for volunteers is closed. The scheduler makes it and keeps only its hash; the portal gets the hashes on the sync, spends the invite at submit, and the scheduler learns of the use from the next pull. An organizer can copy a link (POST /api/admin/portal/invites) or have it emailed (.../invites/send, drawn here).

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor O as Organizer
    participant A as routers/portal_admin.py
    participant PG as Postgres
    participant PS as portal_sync
    participant P as portal routers/sync.py
    participant MR as Mailer → mailrelay
    actor V as Volunteer
    participant S as portal signup.py

    O->>A: POST /api/admin/portal/invites/send {name, email, days}
    A->>A: clean_email, then one send per INVITE_SEND_GAP_SEC (10 s), all organizers
    alt within 10 s of the last send
        A-->>O: 429, Retry-After
    end
    A->>PG: INSERT signup_invites: sha256(token), label, expires NOW() + days, COMMIT
    Note right of A: link = {PORTAL_PUBLIC_URL}/apply/signup?invite=token,<br/>never stored, never returned by send
    A->>PS: push_signup_invites (before the mail, so the link works on arrival)
    PS->>P: POST /api/sync/signup_invites {invites: hashes, content_hash, op_id}
    P->>P: replace the list wholesale, keep used_at, store signup_invites_hash
    A->>PS: send_admin_mail kind signup_invite
    PS->>P: POST /api/sync/send_admin_mail (signed, op_id)
    P->>P: link must start with PORTAL_PUBLIC_URL + /apply/signup?invite=
    P->>P: at most 200 invite mails an hour
    P->>MR: the organizers' invite template (Volunteer Portal → Invite email)
    alt push or mail failed
        A->>PG: DELETE the invite, request_push()
        A-->>O: 429 (portal's hourly cap) or 502
    else sent
        A->>PG: UPDATE emailed_at, audit (label, never the address)
        A-->>O: invite_id, label, expires_at
    end

    V->>S: open /apply/signup?invite=…
    S->>S: GET signup/invite: valid, used, expired or revoked (read-only)
    V->>S: check_email, verify, submit (diagram 4), the invite riding on the login token
    S->>S: submit: _consume_invite in the same transaction as the INSERT
    Note over PS,S: Next tick (diagram 3): the pulled volunteer carries invite_id,<br/>so the scheduler sets used_at and used_by. The signup is still pending.

Revoking (invites/revoke) sets revoked_at and calls request_push(); the portal refuses the link from the next push on.

docs.title: 12. Purging a volunteer
docs.text:
Deleting a volunteer outright, for clearing test signups so their address can sign up again. Inactive volunteers only. The portal goes first: deleted here first, the next pull would bring the volunteer straight back.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor O as Organizer
    participant A as routers/portal_admin.py
    participant PS as portal_sync.purge_volunteers
    participant PG as Postgres
    participant P as portal routers/sync.py
    participant SQ as portal.db
    participant EV as routers/events.py

    O->>A: POST /api/admin/volunteers/purge {vol_ids, confirm}
    A->>A: 1 to PURGE_MAX (500) ids, confirm = the vol_id, or the count
    A->>PG: every id exists and has inactive_at
    alt missing, or still active
        A-->>O: 404, or 409 "make them inactive first"
    end
    A->>PS: purge_volunteers(ids)
    PS->>PS: take _state.lock, the one every sync tick holds
    PS->>PG: SELECT vol_id, portal_rekey_from
    opt portal configured
        PS->>P: POST /api/sync/purge_volunteers {vol_ids + any re-key old ids, op_id}
        P->>SQ: BEGIN IMMEDIATE
        P->>SQ: delete the row, picks, sessions and login_tokens by id or email_hmac
        P->>SQ: clear snapshot_slots, drop the address's rate-limit buckets, audit, COMMIT
        P-->>PS: purged
        alt portal failed in any way
            PS-->>A: RuntimeError, nothing deleted here
            A-->>O: 502, try again
        end
    end
    PS->>PG: _PURGE_LOCAL_SQL: delete picks, shift_flags, vol_notes,<br/>empty vol_id in schedule and radio_checkouts (rows kept)
    PS->>PG: DELETE volunteers RETURNING vol_id, COMMIT
    PS->>PS: release the lock, request_push()
    A->>A: audit each, by name and id
    A->>EV: broadcast("volunteers"), broadcast("schedule")
    A-->>O: purged ids

Because the delete runs under the sync lock, a pull already under way finishes first, and no pull can start between the portal's delete and the scheduler's. Radio history keeps person_name, so a returned radio still says who had it.

docs.title: 13. Passkey sign-in
docs.text:
An organizer signs in with a passkey instead of a password. No username is typed: the authenticator offers whatever passkeys it holds for this site. The session at the end is the one the password login makes, from the same function.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor O as Organizer
    participant L as setup/Login.vue + lib/passkey.js
    participant AU as Authenticator (browser, phone or manager)
    participant PK as routers/passkeys.py
    participant AS as auth.start_session
    participant PG as Postgres

    L->>PK: GET /api/passkeys/config
    PK->>PK: _site(): rp_id = ADMIN_PUBLIC_URL's host (else PORTAL_PUBLIC_URL's)
    PK-->>L: enabled (false when unset, or plain http off localhost)
    Note over L: The button shows only when enabled and the browser has WebAuthn.

    O->>L: Sign in with a passkey
    L->>PK: POST /api/passkeys/login/options
    PK->>PG: sweep expired webauthn_challenges
    PK->>PG: INSERT sha256(challenge), purpose login, no user_id, 5 min, COMMIT
    PK-->>L: options: rp_id, challenge, user verification required
    L->>AU: startAuthentication (@simplewebauthn/browser, lazy-loaded)
    AU->>O: PIN or biometric
    AU-->>L: signed assertion (credential id, userHandle, sign count)
    alt prompt cancelled
        L-->>O: nothing shown (cancelled)
    end

    L->>PK: POST /api/passkeys/login/verify {credential}
    PK->>PG: _consume_challenge: UPDATE SET used_at WHERE unused, unexpired,<br/>purpose login, COMMIT, before any signature check
    alt no such challenge (expired or replayed)
        PK-->>L: 400
    end
    PK->>PG: SELECT user_passkeys JOIN users WHERE credential_id = ?
    alt unknown passkey, or userHandle ≠ users.webauthn_user_id
        PK->>PK: audit
        PK-->>L: 401 "Passkey not recognized. Sign in with your password"
    end
    PK->>PK: verify_authentication_response (challenge, rp_id, origin,<br/>public key, sign count, user verification)
    alt signature or count fails
        PK->>PK: audit
        PK-->>L: 401
    end
    PK->>PG: UPDATE sign_count, backed_up, last_used_at
    PK->>AS: start_session(row)
    AS->>PG: UPDATE users last_login_at, INSERT sessions, COMMIT
    AS->>AS: session cookie, _session_cache entry
    PK->>PK: audit "Signed in with a passkey (alg)"
    PK-->>L: {username, role}, the same as POST /api/login

The challenge burns on the first attempt whether the signature then checks or not, so a captured response is good for nothing. A passkey removed from the account still lives on the device, which keeps offering it; that's the 401 that says to use the password. Adding a passkey (register/options) needs the current password, so a stolen session cookie can't plant one.

docs.title: 14. From a hostile request to an alert
docs.text:
A request to the volunteer portal that looks like an attack, or that the volunteer pages could never have sent, is noticed on the portal, pulled into the scheduler's audit log on the next sync tick, and mailed as an alert. A finding on the organizer site takes the same path from audit() on, without the pull. Nothing here blocks the request, except a NUL, or an anomaly with PORTAL_STRICT=enforce.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor X as Client
    participant SS as portal security_signals.SecuritySignals
    participant V as portal validation.py
    participant SQ as portal.db portal_security_events
    participant L as portal_sync loop
    participant AU as audit.ingest / audit()
    participant AL as alerts.observe
    participant PG as Postgres audit_events
    participant W as alerts worker
    participant P as portal send_admin_mail (kind alert)
    actor O as Organizers with audit_alerts

    X->>SS: POST /api/portal/signup/submit
    SS->>SS: signatures, scanner, probe path, NUL (400), cross-site
    SS->>V: the route runs
    V->>V: strict rules: unknown key, wrong type, name_chars, ...
    alt an anomaly
        V->>SQ: portal.anomaly {rule, where, mode, held_back} (≤ 1/min per client+rule+path)
        Note right of V: enforce: 400 Malformed request<br/>report: the old forgiving path
    end
    SS->>SS: score the response status, once per hour per client
    SS->>SQ: security.attack_signature / suspicious_client / sync_auth_fail
    L->>P: GET /api/sync/heartbeat → security_events_rev
    L->>SQ: GET /api/sync/security_events?since=cursor
    L->>AU: ingest(event, "portal"): checked as untrusted
    AU->>AU: logs/audit.jsonl (json.dumps, ensure_ascii)
    AU->>AL: observe(record)
    AL->>AL: rule by address, cooldown 1 h, held_back counted
    AL->>AU: audit("alert.fired", severity of the rule)
    AU->>PG: INSERT (own connection, own commit), source portal
    AL->>W: queue (≤ 15 mailed an hour)
    W->>P: one per recipient: rule, title, facts (defanged by the portal)
    P->>O: [title] Security alert, link {ADMIN_PUBLIC_URL}/admin/audit
    W->>AU: alert.mailed (a count) or alert.mail_fail (by username)
    Note over AL,W: flush_held_back every 10 min: a "(continued)" alert<br/>for a cooled-down rule with events held back

docs.title: Code quality and security posture
docs.text:
How the BSides code is checked, what blocks a change, how the quality score ratchet works, and where the security protections live in the design. It also lists what nothing checks yet.

Everything here runs locally with one command:

python3 -m pip install -r backend/requirements.txt -r requirements-dev.txt   # once
./run_lint.sh

run_lint.sh runs, in order:

  1. the tests for the dynamic-sql pylint plugin (lint/)
  2. pylint, once per app, code and tests separately
  3. Bandit
  4. mkdocs build --strict

Any failure in any step fails the run. Tests run separately (./run_tests.sh).

docs.title: The three tiers
docs.text:
pylint's findings fall into three tiers. Each tier is handled differently.

Tier What What happens 1. Security The checks in fail-on in .pylintrc Blocks. Any single finding fails the run, in code or tests, whatever the score. 2. Quality and readability Everything else that's enabled: naming, docstrings, complexity, design limits, refactoring hints Reported. Counts against the score; doesn't block on its own. 3. Ratchet A minimum score per app Blocks if the score drops below the app's threshold.

So tier 1 is about what kind of finding, and tier 3 is about how many tier-2 findings there are. Bandit's findings block on their own, whatever the score (see Bandit).

docs.title: Tier 1: security (blocking)
docs.text: Check Catches Why it matters here All E and F messages Errors: undefined names, bad calls, import failures, syntax These are bugs, not style. eval-used, exec-used, bad-builtin eval, exec, compile, __import__, input Running strings as code, or reading a terminal in a server. bare-except, broad-exception-caught except: and except Exception: that swallow the error Swallowed errors hide real failures. The CSV import bug was one: a broad except hid a transaction abort. try-except-raise, lost-exception Handlers that do nothing, return in finally The exception isn't handled the way the code reads. raise-missing-from raise X inside except without from Keeps (or deliberately drops) the cause, so logs show the real failure. dangerous-default-value Mutable default arguments Shared state between calls. subprocess-run-check, subprocess-popen-preexec-fn subprocess.run without check, preexec_fn Ignored exit codes; preexec_fn isn't safe with threads. unspecified-encoding open() without encoding= The default is the platform's. vol_mail runs on organizers' own machines, and on Windows that is cp1252, which crashed on names outside it. consider-using-with Files, zips and so on opened outside with Leaked handles. global-statement global x Module state lives in a small dataclass instance instead (_state, _clock, _config). undefined-loop-variable Using a loop variable after an empty loop Wrong value, or a crash. deprecated-module pickle, cPickle, marshal, shelve, telnetlib Unsafe deserialisation. dynamic-sql SQL text built at runtime (below) SQL injection, by construction.

docs.title: Tier 2: quality and readability
docs.text:
pylint's defaults, plus most of its optional extensions:

  • Complexity: mccabe complexity at most 10.
  • Design limits: at most 6 arguments, 15 locals, 12 branches, 50 statements, 6 returns and 4 nested blocks per function, and 1000 lines per module.
  • Docstrings: Google style. When a docstring has an Args: section, it must match the real signature (docparams). A docstring with no such section is fine.
  • Modern idioms: magic values, X | None over Optional[X], sets for membership tests, and similar.
  • Line length: 100.

Turned off everywhere:

  • too-few-public-methods: Pydantic models.
  • consider-using-assignment-expr: opinionated.
  • fixme: TODOs are listed by ./run_lint.sh --todo instead of counted.

Turned off for test files only (in run_lint.sh), because these are normal pytest idioms:

  • redefined-outer-name, unused-argument: fixtures are injected by parameter name.
  • protected-access: tests poke at module internals on purpose.
  • import-outside-toplevel, wrong-import-position: imports after sys.path or environment setup.
  • missing-function-docstring: the test name is the documentation.
  • magic-value-comparison: asserting on literal expected values is the point.

docs.title: What the score is
docs.text:
pylint rates each run out of 10:

score = 10 − 10 × (5·errors + warnings + refactors + conventions) / statements

Two things follow from the formula:

  • Every tier-2 message lowers the score. An error costs five times as much as anything else.
  • The score is per statement. New code with no findings raises it, so cleaning up and writing clean new code both move it up.

docs.title: How the ratchet works
docs.text:
Each app has two thresholds, one for its code and one for its tests, in the APPS table at the top of run_lint.sh. A run fails if a score falls below its threshold.

App Code: score Code: ratchet Tests: score Tests: ratchet portal 9.02 9.0 9.84 9.8 backend 9.03 9.0 9.79 9.7 mailrelay 8.85 8.8 9.75 9.7 vol_mail 8.62 8.6 9.40 9.3

The root conftest.py scores 10.00 and has no ratchet.

History:

Date Event Code ratchets (portal / backend / mailrelay / vol_mail) 2026-11-18 First baseline, when lint was introduced 8.8 / 8.6 / 8.8 / 8.1 2026-11-18 Raised after the security-tier cleanup (static SQL, state holders, raise … from) 8.9 / 8.8 / 8.8 / 8.6 2026-11-23 Backend raised with the structured audit log (audit.py) 8.9 / 8.9 / 8.8 / 8.6 2026-11-23 Portal and backend raised with security alerts (alerts.py) 9.0 / 9.0 / 8.8 / 8.6

Scores are per app because the apps are linted separately: backend/ and portal/ both have modules called db and main, so one pylint run would resolve imports against the wrong app. That's the same reason run_tests.sh splits the test suites.

docs.title: Why a ratchet rather than "fix everything"
docs.text: The first baseline had about 640 tier-2 messages (730 in all, 87 of them tier 1), most of them long lines, magic values and missing docstrings. Blocking on all of them at once would have meant one enormous change with little to show for it, or turning the checks off. The ratchet makes a different promise: the code doesn't get worse, and it gets better as it's touched.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• Never lower a ratchet to get a change through. If your change lowers the score, fix the messages it introduced. If one is wrong for that case, disable it on that line with a reason (see Accepted exceptions).
  • Raise a ratchet when the score has moved up after a cleanup, in the same commit.
  • Round down to one decimal. pylint shows two decimals and rounds them, so a displayed 8.20 can really be 8.198 and fail a ratchet of 8.2. When the display ends in 0, go one tenth lower. (vol_mail's code ratchet once failed at a displayed 8.20 for exactly this reason.)

docs.title: Useful commands
docs.text:
./run_lint.sh --no-bandit --no-docs                 # just pylint
./run_lint.sh --no-bandit --no-docs -- --fail-on=   # the scores alone, ignoring tier 1
./run_lint.sh --todo                                # also list TODO/FIXME

Run pylint from BSides/ or pass --rcfile=BSides/.pylintrc. Inside an app directory, pylint doesn't find the config: backend/ isn't a package, so its config search stops there.

docs.title: SQL is always a literal
docs.text:
Every SQL statement is one complete string literal, and values go in only as bound ? parameters. Nothing builds SQL text at runtime: no f-strings, +, % or .format(), not even from constants.

A placeholder can stand in for a value. It can't stand in for a table name, a column name, or a piece of SQL. So code that needs a choice uses one of these:

Need Technique Example A constant value, e.g. an expiry Bind it NOW() … + ? * INTERVAL '1 hour' An optional clause A bound flag in a CASE or OR cancelled_at = CASE WHEN ? THEN NULL ELSE cancelled_at END, WHERE (? OR v.is_assignable) One of several tables or columns A dict or tuple of whole literal statements _ALL_KEYS_SQL, _IMAGE_SQL, SNAPSHOT_TABLES A variable-length list (Postgres) An array parameter day_key = ANY(?::text[]) with a Python list; psycopg2 sends a tuple as a row Updating only some columns A "was it sent" flag per column the portal's _UPSERT_VOLUNTEER_SQL A rule shared by many queries Put it in the schema volunteers.is_live / is_counted / is_assignable (migration v17)

Enforcement:

  • dynamic-sql (lint/pylint_sql.py) is in tier 1. It recognises SQL by structure, case-sensitively (SELECT … FROM, INSERT INTO, UPDATE x SET, WHERE, VALUES (, …), and resolves named constants, so _COLS + "FROM users" is caught too. Its tests are in lint/test_pylint_sql.py and run first in every run_lint.sh.
  • Bandit's B608 covers similar ground as a second net. Before the rewrite it missed 4 of the 33 sites.

docs.title: Bandit
docs.text:
Bandit scans for common security problems that pylint doesn't look for: shell injection, unsafe deserialisation, weak cryptography, binding to all interfaces, hardcoded passwords and the like.

  • Application code: every test, failing at medium severity and medium confidence or above.
  • Test files: the same, except B101 (assert), because asserts are how pytest works.
  • Never scanned: Scheduler/ (legacy reference code), frontend/, node_modules/, .venv/.
  • No global skips. Every accepted finding is marked on its own line (below).

Below the threshold, application code currently has only two low-severity B101 findings: asserts that guard against programmer error, not input.

docs.title: Accepted exceptions
docs.text:
Every suppression sits on the line it applies to, with its reason in a comment. This is the full list. Reviewers should question any new entry.

Where Suppresses Reason backend/portal_sync.py (_has_table, ×2) broad-exception-caught Any failure only means "not Postgres", then "no such table". Used by the SQLite tests. backend/portal_sync.py (_sync_once) broad-exception-caught The sync loop must outlive any failure. The error is recorded in portal_sync_state and shown in the Admin UI. backend/routers/invites.py (invite mail) broad-exception-caught A failed mail mustn't undo the invite. The error goes back to the organizer as email_error. backend/routers/password_reset.py broad-exception-caught The reply never varies, so no failure may reach the caller. It's logged and audited. tools/vol_mail/vol_mail.py (decrypt) broad-exception-caught One undecryptable address skips that volunteer, and is reported, without stopping the run. backend/main.py, portal/main.py Bandit B104 Binding to all interfaces inside the container; compose.yml decides what reaches it. mailrelay/relay.py Bandit B104 The same, and the relay has no published ports: only the portal, on mail_internal, can reach it. portal/mailer.py Bandit B310 MAIL_RELAY_URL is refused at startup unless it's http:// or https:// (config.py). docs/gen_export_api.py, lint/test_pylint_sql.py Import position Tooling that imports app code only after setting sys.path.

To list them from the code, so this table can be checked:

grep -rn --include=*.py -E "# nosec|pylint: disable" backend portal mailrelay tools lint docs

docs.title: Security in the design
docs.text:
The lint covers how code is written. Most of the system's protection comes from how it's built. Each of these points is documented in the CLAUDE.md beside the code it describes.

Separation and blast radius

  • The volunteer portal is a separate application on the internet-facing side, with no shared database, session secret or code. If that host is fully compromised, the attacker gets volunteer names, email ciphertext and a copy of the schedule. They don't get organizer credentials, notes, ratings, the scheduler's cookie secret, or any readable email address.
  • Traffic flows only scheduler → portal. The portal has no callback URL, so the scheduler needs no inbound opening.
  • The mail relay is the only process holding the Microsoft Graph credential. It's standard-library only, sends from one hard-coded address, takes exactly to / subject / body, is rate-limited, has a read-only filesystem except /state, and has no published ports.

Secrets and personal data

  • Email addresses are stored as RSA-OAEP ciphertext. The private key never leaves an organizer's machine: .rsync-filter keeps *.pem off the server. A keyed HMAC acts as the lookup index, and its key lives only in the environment, never in a database.
  • Only hashes are stored for login links, sessions, invite and reset links, and export API keys (SHA-256). A copy of a database isn't enough to mint a session or call the API.
  • Audit logs carry ids, never addresses. There are tests for this.

Authentication

  • Export API: scoped bearer keys with an expiry (at most 365 days) and an optional IP allow-list.
  • Every failure gets the same bare 401, and 10 failures per IP in 15 minutes give a 429.
  • Calls are audited by key label, never by the key itself.
  • It sends no CORS headers.
  • Sync API: HMAC-signed requests, a ±300 s timestamp window, a nonce table against replay, and an op_id on every POST so a retry can't apply twice.
  • Organizer sign-in: a password or a passkey.
  • Adding a passkey needs the current password.
  • WebAuthn challenges are single-use.
  • Password-reset replies never vary and are rate-limited.
  • Completing a reset signs the account out everywhere.
  • Links aren't spent by a GET, so mail scanners and link previews can't use up a token.

Organizer-edited content

  • Templates (the landing page, the invite email) render in Jinja's sandbox, and a parse- tree check allows only variables, {% if %}, comparisons and a few text filters, so a template can't reach other objects or loop forever. Both apps check this: the scheduler when it's saved, the portal again on every push.
  • The landing page's Markdown is rendered with raw HTML and images off and only web, email and same-site links, because it's inserted into a public page as HTML.

Detection and alerting

  • An audit log (backend/audit.py): every write, sign-in and refusal is one JSON line in logs/audit.jsonl and a row in audit_events. Caller-supplied text can't forge a line.
  • Failed password sign-ins are rate limited per username and address, counting only failures, and an unknown username takes as long to refuse as a wrong password.
  • Request signals (security_signals.py, the same file in both apps) watch for attack patterns, scanners, probing, malformed input, cross-site writes and forged session cookies. They only watch: the one request refused is one carrying a NUL.
  • Strict portal input (portal/validation.py): the volunteer pages check every field by the portal's own rules before sending, from one shared list of cases both test suites run, so input that breaks them is an anomaly: recorded and alerted on, and refused once PORTAL_STRICT=enforce.
  • Alerts (backend/alerts.py) turn those, and account and key changes, into email to the organizers ticked for security alerts, at most once an hour per cause. The portal sends them through a fixed template with every detail defanged.

Runtime

  • Images: Alpine base images, with no build tools or curl in them.
  • Users: the Python services run as non-root users (uid 1001; the mail relay as 10001).

docs.title: Known gaps
docs.text:
What nothing checks today, roughly in order of value:

  • Dependency vulnerabilities, between scans. tools/sbom.sh scans every image and library with trivy, and the Security pages show the result. It runs by hand, though, so the page is only as current as its "as of" date, and nothing fails a build on a new CVE. The Python libraries are pinned to their current major version, not to exact versions, so two builds a month apart can differ in patch and minor releases.
  • Secrets in the repository. No secret scanner. .gitignore lists .env and its backups, *.pem, *.key and api_key*, and .rsync-filter keeps keys off the server (.env syncs on purpose). Nothing checks file contents, though. Run a scanner such as gitleaks before pushing. See Secrets and keys.
  • Changing a password doesn't end other sessions. Changing your own password, or an organizer setting one, increments users.password_version, but nothing reads that column. Other signed-in sessions, and the backend's session cache, carry on. Only a password reset by email deletes the account's sessions.
  • The frontend. The Vue/JavaScript code has no linter or security scanner.
  • Requests nginx answers itself. On the public hostname, nginx 404s everything outside /, /apply/ and /api/portal/, so a scanner's tries at /wp-login.php or /.env reach no app and raise no signal. Only nginx's own access log has them.
  • A session that moves. Nothing notices a session cookie used from a new network part-way through a session (a stolen cookie). sessions.ip_addr holds the real client address since 1.1, so the check can be added; it isn't yet.
  • Portal strict mode starts in report. Until PORTAL_STRICT=enforce, input the volunteer pages can't send is alerted on but still accepted.
  • Detection never blocks. A client that sets off alerts keeps being served until an organizer does something about it. That's deliberate (an automatic block can lock an organizer out on event day), but it means the alerts are the defence, not a wall.
  • Types. No type checker (mypy or pyright). Annotations aren't verified.
  • Tooling code. docs/ and lint/ aren't in run_lint.sh's app list. The plugin is tested, but neither directory is linted.
  • Postgres-only tests skip unless TEST_PG_HOST is set, so ./run_tests.sh alone doesn't run them. That's 205 of the backend's 376 tests (as of November 2026), including every export, invite, passkey, CSV import, migration, audit-table and Audit Log test. backend/CLAUDE.md → Tests explains how to start a throwaway Postgres for them.
  • Broad catches that re-raise. pylint's broad-exception-caught ignores a handler that raises, so two are unflagged:
  • backend/routers/invites.py (invite acceptance) reports any database error as "username is taken". It should catch psycopg2.errors.UniqueViolation only.
  • portal/routers/sync.py (branding push) treats any exception as malformed base64.
  • MkDocs. The project behind MkDocs 1.x is no longer maintained upstream (the build prints a warning about it). It works today; replacing it is a decision for later.
  • Live testing. Nothing here runs against the deployed stack. The shell scripts in backend/ (test_grid.sh, test_radios.sh, test_categories.sh) do, and need credentials.

docs.title: Organizer guide
docs.text:
This guide is for organizers running the event on the admin site. It follows the order of the season: set up, open signup, approve and schedule volunteers, send schedules, then run the event days.

The admin site is at the admin hostname, behind a sign-in gate. Its toolbar has three menus: Call for Volunteers, Admin, and your own name on the right, with Profile and Sign Out. Below the toolbar are three tabs: Schedule, Volunteers and Radios.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text: Role For Can do organizer the volunteer team everything checkin the check-in desk and radio table check volunteers in, rate them, issue and return radios view anyone who only needs to look read only

docs.title: First-time setup
docs.text:
A fresh install opens the setup wizard:

  1. Create the admin account, the first organizer. This step locks once any account exists.
  2. Sign in.
  3. Your conference: its name, and how volunteers can reach you: a contact email, the conference website and its code of conduct. Then the logo. The volunteer pages show all of them, and leave out anything blank. Everything can be skipped and changed later in Admin → App Settings.
  4. Set up the schedule. Either build it in the wizard (days, then categories, then times, then a grid of how many people each position needs at each time) or import a CSV.
  5. Import volunteers from a CSV, or skip this and let them sign up.

Then, before opening signup:

  • Admin → Email Key: upload the organizers' public key. Signup can't open without it. Secrets explains the key pair.
  • Admin → App Settings: set the event timezone, which check-in uses to judge early or late.
  • Admin → Users: add the other organizers, or use Invite Someone to send a link that lets them make their own account. Invite links last 72 hours.

docs.title: Editing the schedule
docs.text:
Edit Schedule on the Schedule tab opens the editor:

  • Categories: their order and chip colors.
  • Days: each day, its date, and which times it runs.
  • Times: each time range, and the days it runs on.
  • Grid: how many of each position at each day and time. Changes are applied as a difference. A slot with a volunteer assigned is never removed; the editor lists it instead.

docs.title: Signup
docs.text:
Open Call for Volunteers → Volunteer Portal:

  • Volunteer signup open/closed is the switch. Signup also shows as closed while there's no email key, and as full when no two timeslots with space remain.
  • Overbook by lets more volunteers pick a timeslot than it has slots, to make up for people who drop out. Volunteers see the inflated space. Shift Demand shows the real numbers.
  • Early access invites let one person sign up while signup is closed. Make a link to send yourself, or use Send invites by email. Each link works once.
  • The sync status shows when the portal last answered, and any error. Sync now runs a pass at once.

docs.title: What the volunteer pages say
docs.text:
The same dialog has three more tabs for the words volunteers see. Each has Save and Reset to default, and the portal has a saved change within a few seconds.

  • Landing page: the public call for volunteers. It's three Markdown parts (the intro above the two buttons, the main column and the sidebar) plus the opportunity cards, each with an icon, a name and a line of text. {{ conference }}, {{ contact_email }}, {{ conference_url }} and {{ code_of_conduct_url }} fill in from App Settings, and {% if contact_email %}…{% endif %} leaves a sentence out when it's blank. Preview shows it as volunteers will see it. Raw HTML, images and links other than web pages and email addresses are left out.
  • Questionnaire: the signup form's questions, in order. For each one, choose its type (choice, dropdown, checkbox, acknowledgement or text), the signup step it's on, whether it's required, and whether volunteers can change their answer later. Choices can ask a follow-up when picked. You can change the questions at any time. Removing one keeps the answers already given, and the editor tells you how many there are first. The flexible question is used by the assignment picker: you can reword or remove it, but it stays a checkbox. Don't ask for anything sensitive, because answers are stored as plain text.
  • Invite email: the subject and body of the early-access invite. It's a template, with {{ first_name }}, {{ conference }}, {{ link }}, {{ expires }} and the App Settings values, plus {% if %}…{% else %}…{% endif %}. The body must include {{ link }}. Preview fills in an invented volunteer.

Call for Volunteers → Shift Demand shows, for each timeslot, how many slots exist, how many are open, how many volunteers picked it, and how much space is left.

docs.title: Approving volunteers
docs.text:
New signups wait at the top of the Volunteers tab, under Pending Volunteers, with their picks, their answers, and any existing volunteer whose name looks similar.

  • Approve makes them active, so they can be assigned. You can give them a badge number as their id at the same time.
  • Make inactive declines them. They stay on file, so the same address can't simply sign up again.

Approval doesn't schedule anyone. Picks stay preferences until you assign them.

docs.title: The volunteer list
docs.text:
The rest of the Volunteers tab lists everyone, whatever their status, with their picks, answers and shifts.

  • Make inactive and Reinstate take someone off the schedule pickers and put them back. Their assignments stay. While they're inactive, those slots show as needing a replacement.
  • Decrypt emails asks for the private key, pasted or chosen from a file, and adds an Email column. Addresses are decrypted in this browser only. The key isn't sent anywhere, and Forget key clears it from the page.
  • Add Volunteer adds someone by hand. Their address is encrypted in the browser before it's sent.
  • Purge deletes an inactive volunteer outright, here and on the portal. Use it to clear test volunteers, so their addresses can sign up again from scratch.
